title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
description: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred"
body: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used. It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess". She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology."All I wanted was justice," Martinez said. Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.

schema.headline: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution

title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
description: US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.Shares in
body: US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.Shares in Intel continued their overnight slide into early trading on Friday, falling as much as 30% after the chip maker warned of a weaker computer market even as it plans to increase spending on AI.Amazon shares fell as far as 6% before recovering after its reported earnings on Thursday evening fell short of investors' expectations.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange opened on Friday at its lowest level in more than two months, down 2.5%, as other tech stocks including Reddit and Roblox continued to fall.The losses follow the value of Google owner Alphabet plunging by more than $500bn on Thursday after it revealed its own AI summaries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 1% after Thursday's massive slide.The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value after its earnings update rattled investors.On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year, and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter."Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.Amazon on Thursday revealed the company was also spending more cash that it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.Shares in Amazon recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out"."The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

schema.headline: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears

title: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine
description: A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline regi
body: A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water."Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning."At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa. They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind."The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise." Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter. "She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said."That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

schema.headline: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine

title: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
description: The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters
body: The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus"."Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said."The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing. Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information". In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form. Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov, external. In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.At the offices of Novaya Gazeta, they've already started packing.The end of this newspaper is very much the end of an era.In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

schema.headline: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities

title: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, US Senator Chris MurphyByTom Bateman State department correspondentA top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, US Senator Chris MurphyByTom Bateman State department correspondentA top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked. "The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.Image source, ReutersImage caption, US President Donald Trump at a meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-SisiWashington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".Image source, Egyptian Initiative for Personal RightsImage caption, Six journalists from the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh who were arrested in Egypt and are facing terrorism chargesRubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza. Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue."To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI."Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Amnesty International called the verdict against Lina Attalah 'a crushing blow to press freedom' (file photo)The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt, external as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists. The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country."It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC."Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

schema.headline: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision

title: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions
description: Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison
body: Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said."We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.

schema.headline: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) wa
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.The company also told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".Binance had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling. It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

schema.headline: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea

title: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
description: Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hittin
body: Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term."I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.By the end of Thursday,  the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race. But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours  trading.Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools."One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added."We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI."Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

schema.headline: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales

title: Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
description: A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.A
body: A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.Andreas Malm told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had received a letter from the Home Office notifying him that his presence was "not conducive to the public good", with no further details given.He said he could not "see any other explanation" for being denied entry than his scheduled appearance with Huda Ammori, a founder of the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.The Home Office said it did not comment on individual cases.Malm is a senior lecturer in human ecology at Sweden's Lund University, whose work includes the 2021 book How to Blow up a Pipeline and 2025's The Destruction of Palestine is the Destruction of the Earth.He said he had asked the Home Office to explain its decision, but could not see a reason beyond the upcoming talk in London with Ammori organised by the left-wing magazine Tribune - calling the move a "severe restriction on the free exchange of ideas".Malm said he was not a member of Palestine Action, had never publicly endorsed it, nor had he given it any financial support."The only link to Palestine Action is her as a person," he said, criticising the UK government for ascribing "guilt by association".The academic acknowledged that he had previously described the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel - in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage - as "fundamentally an act of liberation".Malm said it was possible that these remarks, during a December 2023 talk in which he also condemned the "deplorable" killing of civilians in the cross-border attack, had been the reason for the Home Office's decision.But he argued that these views had been in the public realm for a long time, including when he was last allowed into the UK to deliver a talk in May."I don't expect the British state to agree with me on Palestine or climate or anything. What I expect the British state to do is to continue to let me enter the country and to discuss with colleagues, with people who disagree with me - as I have done for years."

schema.headline: Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder

title: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
description: China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless
body: China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times, external.The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.Nvidia said their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.The BBC has contacted Megaspeed and the White House for comment.US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry. But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".Megaspeed told the paper its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate. It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

schema.headline: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO

title: New York police will investigate all sex crimes at Cornell, governor says
description: Hochul said New York State Police signed an agreement with Cornell University so that all sexual offence complaints, which had historically fallen und
body: Hochul said New York State Police signed an agreement with Cornell University so that all sexual offence complaints, which had historically fallen under the jurisdiction of university police, will be immediately referred to state police instead."When someone reports sexual assault," Hochul said on Thursday, they deserve "to know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated by law enforcement trained to support survivors"."Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them," the governor added. Backlash against the Ivy League university has been intense since Jane Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September. On Wednesday, the institution's Faculty Senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff, met behind closed-doors and decided to move forward with voting on a resolution of no-confidence against the administration and the university's President Michael Kotlikoff.The vote will be open for faculty starting on Friday and run until 6 November. The vote is largely symbolic but could intensify pressure on changing the university's leadership. Earlier this month, the university announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including adding sexual assault investigators to its police force. Hochul had said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, earlier this month to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.The woman at the centre of the case filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.

schema.headline: New York police will investigate all sex crimes at Cornell, governor says

title: Von der Leyen lays out vision for new Canada-EU partnership at Montreal summit
description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her vision for what an "associate membership" status for Canada to the EU would look l
body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her vision for what an "associate membership" status for Canada to the EU would look like as officials gather in Montreal to discuss closer ties. It is "a partnership that comes close to membership than anything we have done before," she said on Thursday's remarks at the two-day Canada-EU summit.She added it is a type of relationship that would be open "only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together."It includes close alignment on governance and policies, and partnering in research and innovation. For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this year's meeting in the Canadian city.  Thursday and Friday's summit is being closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.Von der Leyen first proposed "opening the door" to Canada last month for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship. Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month. While there is broad support for closer ties, the concept of "associate membership" is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada, he said."Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.Despite some opposition, von der Leyen has continued to use the term has not addressed the disagreement over the term. Later on Thursday, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days. Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months. But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic. Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties."The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit. Polls show the majority of Canadians support forging closer ties to Europe, external, though the Conservative opposition in Canada has criticised the effort as a distraction from other issues, like the high cost of living. "No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," said Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre in a statement, adding that Canada already has a free trade pact with the EU. Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer. US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway. Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme. It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.On Thursday, Canada released its new National Security Strategy, the first in two decades, which underlines supporting security and stability in Europe as a priority.As for what this new relationship status will be called, Carney has said the "nomenclature" does not matter. "What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

schema.headline: Von der Leyen lays out vision for new Canada-EU partnership at Montreal summit

title: From green card to fraud: Kenyans arrested in $130m US ghost student scam
description: In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the worl
body: In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya. The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds. US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved."If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue. "The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college."His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.The scale of the suspected fraud is significant. Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses."In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya. In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000  from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya. The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid. Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.You may also be interested in:

schema.headline: From green card to fraud: Kenyans arrested in $130m US ghost student scam

title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
description: The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare
body: The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones."Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed.""I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said."People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week."They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said."This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive." On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable."Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground. "An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon. But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.But the clock is ticking. The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said. "We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months."These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

schema.headline: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next

title: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations
description: Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-pre
body: Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.They have made some bold promises. Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down. Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast."In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade."While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC."Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list."Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

schema.headline: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations
